intent: Baseline geometry for a fast line follower. Five 12 mm sensors spread 0.16 m across, 0.04 m ahead of the axle, cover the tape with redundancy, and weights scale with sensor x so the signal is linear in lateral offset. Expected result: completion on the oval and s-bend, with rms error and line-loss events as the main things to watch. If rms error is high on the slalom, I expect to narrow the sensor spread or move the sensors further forward. If the robot oscillates, I expect to reduce wheel track or raise mass for stability. The Integrator should tune gains, not geometry, on this first race.
learning: No prior evidence yet. Hypotheses to test: (1) a 0.04 m forward sensor offset gives enough lead to reduce oscillation without extra derivative gain; (2) five sensors at 0.02 m spacing keep the line in view on the tightest slalom bends; (3) a 0.12 m wheel track is wide enough for stable turning at base speed 2.0. Next iteration I want to see whether rms error is dominated by sensor spacing or by the controller's lag.
rationale: This is the first iteration, so there is no race telemetry or Integrator feedback yet. The design therefore starts from the contract's physics and the scoring rule, not from measured results. The race must cover about 4 to 5 m in under 3 s, so the robot needs a fast, stable platform, and the line-following score rewards low RMS error and no line losses. I chose five sensors spread across 0.08 m at 0.02 m spacing. That covers roughly the 25 mm tape width with redundancy, so the line is seen even on tight bends. A 12 mm footprint gives each sensor a clear reading of the tape edge without washing out the signal. Sensors sit 0.04 m ahead of the axle so the control signal leads the wheels and gives the Integrator some phase lead against the drivetrain lag. Weights are proportional to sensor x (±2, ±1, 0), so the signal is positive when the line is on the left, matching the contract's steering sign. Wheel track 0.12 m and radius 0.03 m give a moderate turn authority and speed. Mass 0.8 kg with a 0.16 m body keeps yaw inertia low enough to turn quickly. Body width 0.14 m keeps the off-track limit at its 0.06 m floor. I expect this to complete the course with few line losses, though I expect rms error to be the main cost. The base speed is set at 2.0 (full voltage) so the speed target is met, and the gains are moderate. Those gains belong to the Integrator, so I only list them as guidance in the intent.
